title: Mark Zuckerberg says the future of AI is for everyone. But who owns it?
excerpt: It’s a nice sentiment, but all AI users should ask three questions about their preferred choice of AI platform
content_html:
On Monday, Mark Zuckerberg published a 6,500-word essay, The Future Is for Everyone. The essay came with something even rarer: a new Meta open-weight model. An open-weight AI model is the kind of AI with which you download the entire thing, and it works on your own computer (with or without the internet) and nobody can switch it off except for you. Almost every mainstream AI tool you use, whether it be Gemini, ChatGPT or Claude, is one you rent access to. Meta’s is one that you can download and actually own. I downloaded it before I finished the essay. So can you.

This major move by the world’s largest tech heavyweight comes amid a summer heavy with AI news, full of nations at war. Washington against Beijing; tech founder against tech founder. But beneath those conflicts is a deeper contest between two kinds of power: a government that can order technology offline in an instant, and a company that can simply close your account. Neither is necessarily villainous. But the rest of us are not merely the audience in this fight; we are the prize. And the terms are already being written: intelligence on lease, a future we pay for but never quite own.

Before you sign a lease, you generally wonder three things. Can I be thrown out? When I go, what goes with me? And if the landlord loses interest, who keeps the place standing? Ask the same three questions of any technology that says it belongs to everyone.

Start with eviction. In 2009, Amazon reached into people’s Kindles overnight and deleted a book that everyone who bought it thought they owned. Nineteen Eighty-Four. On 12 June of this year, the US government did the same thing to AI: three days after the American lab Anthropic launched its most capable model, an order from Washington forced it offline for everyone, everywhere. Within days of Anthropic’s release, I tried two Chinese open-weight models, Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2. I could download them. I could run them myself – and nobody could reach into my server and delete them. On several of my tasks, they performed nearly as well. As such, the deciding question on open or closed models is no longer capability; it is who has the power to switch it off.

The second question is one Zuckerberg’s essay never asks: can you take it with you? The essay does make a real privacy commitment. It introduces a fully private mode, sealed the way WhatsApp is, where even Meta can’t reach. The landlord will be locked out by architecture, and not simply by a promise. But read carefully. The agent he describes will hold your health, stories of your children and years of your thoughts – all in a diary kept in someone else’s house. Ask again: can you take it with you?

And the third question: when the landlord loses interest, who keeps the place standing? Zuckerberg says Chinese models are leading on open-source AI because American labs face heavier data rules. That’s not quite the full story. Chinese labs open their models because openness is their business model. American labs, on the other hand, keep theirs closed because openness would undercut them. Meta was the exception – until it paused its open strategy last year. But then something remarkable happened: absolutely nothing. Everyone who had downloaded Meta’s models kept them, and just kept building. Companies can change their minds, but they cannot undownload a model from somebody else’s machine. The files people had saved kept the ecosystem alive, not the company’s goodwill.

We’ve seen this pattern before. Decades ago, one company gave a free browser to billions – and that act almost closed the web. Internet Explorer was “for everyone” too. What saved the open web was not a better company stepping in, but software built to work for the use, rather than whoever made it. Mozilla exists because of this fight. And this current battle over AI is the sequel.

So everyone using AI should have three demands – and none of them is “pick a better company to trust”.

Hold. Washington already gets this – when Washington itself is the tenant. Its own security posture warns against AI that an outside company could easily switch off. Britain, Canada and Germany already spend significant money on sovereign computing. Extend these principles to civilian life, and critical services like hospitals and government agencies should be required to hold legally usable copies of capable open-weight models, along with the tools and computing capacity to run them. All should face rigorous security and safety testing, whether they come from China, the US or anywhere else. Test the capability, don’t ban the method.

Take. Demand of agents what we just won from models: portability. The memory a machine has of you should be exportable to a rival. The diary should not be trapped in the house. This is the fight that will define the decade.

Build. Openness shouldn’t depend on one company’s willingness to keep sharing. We need to pool the nuts-and-bolts of open-source infrastructure – the testing labs, the harnesses that run the models and the standards – so that the open ecosystem has what the web has today: a foundation that no single company can switch off.

Zuckerberg’s title is right: the future should be for everyone. Open models don’t eliminate dependency; they give us what digital infrastructure rarely provides – a real, practical way to walk away.

  • Raffi Krikorian is the CTO of Mozilla

content_html_zh:
周一，马克·扎克伯格发表了一篇 6,500 字的文章《未来属于每个人》。 这篇文章附带了一些更罕见的东西：一个新的 Meta 开放权重模型。 开放式人工智能模型是一种可以下载整个内容的人工智能，它可以在你自己的计算机上运行（无论有没有互联网），除了你之外没有人可以将其关闭。 几乎你使用的每一种主流人工智能工具，无论是 Gemini、ChatGPT 还是 Claude，都是你可以租用的。 Meta 是您可以下载并实际拥有的一款。 我在写完这篇文章之前就下载了它。 你也可以。

全球最大的科技重量级人物的这一重大举措是在人工智能新闻充斥、国家处于战争状态的夏季发生的。 华盛顿对抗北京；科技创始人对抗科技创始人。 但在这些冲突的背后，是两种权力之间更深层次的竞争：一个可以立即下令技术离线的政府，另一个可以简单地关闭你的帐户的公司。 两者都不一定是邪恶的。 但我们其他人不仅仅是这场战斗的观众；我们也是这场战斗的观众。我们就是奖品。 条款已经写好：租赁情报，我们为之付费但从未完全拥有的未来。

在签署租约之前，您通常会想知道三件事。 我可以被赶出去吗？ 当我走的时候，我会带走什么？ 如果房东失去兴趣，谁来维持这个地方？ 对于任何声称属于所有人的技术，都提出同样的三个问题。

从驱逐开始。 2009年，亚马逊一夜之间侵入了人们的Kindle，删除了一本所有购买过它的人都认为自己拥有的书。 十九点八十四分。 今年 6 月 12 日，美国政府对人工智能做了同样的事情：美国实验室 Anthropic 推出其最强大的模型三天后，华盛顿的一项命令迫使该模型对任何地方的所有人都下线。 Anthropic 发布后几天，我尝试了两款中国开放重量模型，Kimi K3 和 GLM 5.2。 我可以下载它们。 我可以自己运行它们——没有人可以进入我的服务器并删除它们。 在我的一些任务中，他们的表现几乎同样好。 因此，决定开放或封闭模型的问题不再是能力，而是能力。谁有权力将其关闭。

第二个问题是扎克伯格的文章从未问过的一个问题：你能随身携带吗？ 这篇文章确实做出了真正的隐私承诺。 它引入了完全私密的模式，就像 WhatsApp 一样密封，甚至 Meta 也无法到达。 房东将被建筑拒之门外，而不仅仅是因为承诺。 但请仔细阅读。 他所描述的代理人将记录你的健康状况、你孩子的故事以及你多年来的想法——所有这些都记录在别人家里的日记中。 再问：可以随身携带吗？

第三个问题：当房东失去兴趣时，谁来维持这个地方？ 扎克伯格表示，中国模型在开源人工智能领域处于领先地位，因为美国实验室面临更严格的数据规则。 这还不是完整的故事。 中国实验室开放他们的模型，因为开放是他们的商业模式。 另一方面，美国实验室则保持关闭，因为开放会削弱他们的实力。 Meta 是个例外——直到去年它暂停了开放战略。 但随后发生了一件值得注意的事情：什么也没有发生。 每个下载了 Meta 模型的人都会保留它们，并继续构建。 公司可以改变主意，但他们无法从别人的机器上取消下载模型。 人们保存的文件使生态系统保持活力，而不是公司的商誉。

我们以前见过这种模式。 几十年前，一家公司向数十亿人提供了免费浏览器，这一行为几乎导致了网络的关闭。 Internet Explorer 也“适合所有人”。 拯救开放网络的并不是更好的公司介入，而是为使用而构建的软件，而不是制造它的人。 Mozilla 因这场斗争而存在。 当前这场关于人工智能的战斗是续集。

因此，每个使用人工智能的人都应该有三个需求——其中没有一个是“选择一家更好的值得信赖的公司”。

抓住。 华盛顿已经明白了这一点——当华盛顿本身就是租户时。 它自己的安全态势警告外部公司可以轻易关闭人工智能。 英国、加拿大和德国已经在主权计算上投入了大量资金。 将这些原则延伸到平民生活中，并且应该要求医院和政府机构等关键服务拥有合法可用的开放重量模型副本，以及运行这些模型的工具和计算能力。 所有人都应该接受严格的安全测试，无论它们来自中国、美国还是其他任何地方。 测试能力，不要禁止方法。

拿。 代理商的需求正是我们刚刚从模型中赢得的：可移植性。 机器拥有的关于你的内存应该可以导出给竞争对手。 日记不应该被困在房子里。 这场斗争将决定这个十年。

建造。 开放不应该取决于一家公司是否愿意继续分享。 我们需要汇集开源基础设施的具体细节——测试实验室、运行模型和标准的工具——以便开放生态系统拥有当今网络所拥有的一切：一个任何一家公司都无法关闭的基础。

扎克伯格的标题是正确的：未来应该属于每个人。 开放模型并不能消除依赖性；它们为我们提供了数字基础设施很少提供的东西——一种真正、实用的离开方式。

  • Raffi Krikorian 是 Mozilla 的首席技术官
